title: Theodora Refuses to Flee
text:
In January 532 the rival chariot-racing factions of Constantinople, the Blues and the Greens, united against the emperor Justinian. What began as anger over executions and taxes became the Nika riot, named after the rioters' cry, "Conquer!" For days the crowds burned large parts of the city, including the great church of Hagia Sophia, and proclaimed a new emperor, Hypatius.

The historian Procopius, who was in the city, says that Justinian and his advisers met in the palace to decide whether to escape by ship. The empress Theodora then spoke. She said that this was not the time to argue whether a woman should speak among men. Flight, even if it brought safety, was not to be chosen; anyone born must die, but one who had been an emperor should not become a fugitive. If the emperor wished to save himself, there was the sea and there were the ships. As for her, she held to an old saying that royalty is a good burial shroud.

Justinian stayed. His generals Belisarius and Mundus led troops into the Hippodrome, where the rebels had gathered, and massacred them. Procopius says more than thirty thousand died. Hypatius was executed, and Justinian ruled for another thirty-three years.
lesson: In a moment of panic, one steady voice that refuses to run can change everyone's decision. Calm resolve is contagious.
source: Procopius, History of the Wars, Book 1, chapter 24
caveat: Procopius probably shaped Theodora's speech in a literary way, and his death toll is likely exaggerated.
